slots.overviewDescription: High-level view of a production ML system in four stages arranged in a loop: make the model, ship it, run it, and watch it, with a feedback loop from watching back to making.
slots.mapDescription: Architecture map of a production ML system: users feed a data warehouse, training happens on a laptop from a frozen extract, CI/CD ships through GitHub to AWS EC2, a prediction service and nightly batch scoring share one prediction function, an S3 artifact store sits in the middle, and drift monitoring alerts Slack and feeds a dashboard.
slots.legend: Model building Deployment Serving Monitoring & the world Artifacts & storage Dashed groups show where components run
slots.completionLessons:
• Why each of the four stages exists
  • How a model reaches a live API and a nightly job
  • How it fails quietly, and what catches it
slots.completionIntro: You've seen how a production ML system works, end to end. You can now explain:

panels.introHtml:
Start here

You trained a model. Now what?

In a notebook, a model is an answer. In production, it is a promise: fresh predictions for anyone who asks, every day, without you in the room.

Keeping that promise takes a system. This is what one actually looks like, drawn from a real model (it predicts which free trials will convert to paid) with the real tools: AWS, MLflow, GitHub, FastAPI, Docker.

Four stages. Each one exists to remove you from a loop you are currently standing in.

Ways in

  • Open a stage to see what lives inside it.
  • Play a flow above to watch data move through the system.
  • Step the build order (steps 1 to 6) to watch it assemble.
  • Watch it break: one flow follows a failure that never raises an error.
panels.overviewHtml:
The full map

Every component earns its place

This is the whole system: a trial-to-paid conversion model, from warehouse table to a Slack alert that fires on its own.

How to read it

Color is a role: blue makes the model, violet ships it, teal serves predictions, green watches the system and stands in for the world. Amber marks artifacts and their store. Document and bucket icons distinguish the files that move between pipelines from the processes that create them.

Dashed outlines are environments: the product's data platform, your laptop, GitHub, and the always-on instance in the cloud. Most of what makes production feel foreign is just work crossing from one to another.

Click any component for the full story. The ones with real machinery inside (the pipeline, the service, the bucket, tracking, CI, the drift check) have a Look inside button that opens them up.
panels.stageNote: The rest of the map is dimmed, not gone: every stage only makes sense because of what it feeds. Click any lit component to go deeper.
panels.repository: Where this lives in the repo
panels.pinnedNote: Everything on the map is what exists so far. Earlier steps keep running underneath this one.
panels.buildNote: Dashed components don't exist yet. Everything lit was built in an earlier step and keeps running.

ui.flowComplete: Flow complete. Click any component on the path to go deeper, or play another flow.

make.title: Make the model
make.line2: a model you can rebuild and trust.
make.text: Everything here exists to answer one question: could you rebuild this model, exactly, next month? Data is pulled once and frozen, features and training run as code instead of notebook cells, every experiment is logged, and the output is a file on disk rather than a memory in a kernel.

ship.title: Ship it
ship.line1: Turn the model into a container
ship.text: A model on your laptop helps nobody. This step packages the service into a container and automates the path from a git push to a running server: lint, pull the model, test, build, deploy. The same image runs identically on a laptop and in the cloud, and no human touches the server.

run.title: Run it
run.line2: who asks, on demand or on schedule.
run.text: The paying-off stage. An API answers one trial at a time in milliseconds, a nightly job scores the day's new trials for the morning list, and both share a single prediction function, so the logic exists once. The artifact store in the middle is the shelf every machine reaches for.

watch.title: Watch it
watch.line2: and hear about it before users do.
watch.text: Models fail quietly. This step gives the system senses: every prediction is logged, incoming data is compared against what training saw, drift raises a Slack alert on its own, and one dashboard shows the whole system's health. While labels mature, drift is the early warning; once they arrive, predictions are judged against reality.

overviewEdges.label: when it drifts: retrain, and ship again

nodes.what: People using the product. Every session and every action becomes an event, lands in the analytics warehouse, and eventually becomes a row a model can learn from. New trials start every day, whether or not anyone is watching.
nodes.why: The one component you do not build and cannot control. Everything the system promises downstream, fresh scores, honest monitoring, depends on data that keeps arriving from here, and on it continuing to look enough like the past for the model to make sense of it. When that stops being true, drift detection is how the system finds out.
nodes.tools: No tool plays this seat. In diagrams it is easy to forget; in production it is the whole point.
nodes.bootcampNote: A cohort can't generate live traffic, so a course-run simulator stands in for real users: it writes each day's new trial cohort as a file to a shared bucket, and your system pulls it. On a job, this seat is your product's actual users and nobody operates a knob behind them.

nodes.what: The product's analytics database, where usage events land continuously. A view flattens the events to one row per trial: how much the trial used the product in its first three days plus, once known, whether it converted to paid. Training pulled from it once; the nightly scorer queries it fresh every day.
nodes.why: Every ML system starts as somebody's table. The warehouse is where training data comes from, but it is a moving target: rows keep maturing and definitions change. That is exactly why nothing downstream reads it directly at training time.
nodes.decision: Pull training data once, save the extract, and never depend on the live database again. The warehouse is an origin story, not a runtime dependency.
nodes.tools: Here: Postgres. Same role: Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift.
nodes.bootcampNote: In the course this is a read-only Postgres we host for you, with credentials handed out in Week 0. On a job it is your company's warehouse and getting access is sometimes the hardest step. The queries you wrote are the same either way.

nodes.what: The training data, materialized to a file and stamped with its snapshot date. Pulled once by a small fetch script into the project's data directory; gitignored, reproducible.
nodes.why: Training from a live table means two runs of the same code can produce different models. A frozen extract makes every model traceable to the exact data that shaped it. It also becomes the most durable artifact in the system: a copy is published to the bucket as the drift reference, so that long after training, the system remembers what the world looked like when the model learned it.
nodes.decision: Reproducibility over freshness at training time.
nodes.tools: Here: a dated CSV. Same role: DVC-tracked data, Delta Lake snapshots, a feature store's point-in-time reads.

nodes.what: Every training run logs its parameters, metrics and model artifact. Runs are compared in a UI, and the chosen model is registered as a named version. The tracking server is lightweight: early on it runs wherever the team works, with the heavy artifacts in S3; growing teams move it to a shared instance or a managed platform.
nodes.why: Without tracking, "which model is in production and how was it trained" has no answer. Tracking makes experiments citable: the XGBoost versus logistic regression comparison stops being a memory and becomes a record anyone can audit or rerun.
nodes.decision: The registry is the system of record, not a runtime dependency. Production never calls it; the deployable model is published to S3 as a plain file. Some real teams do deploy straight from the registry; keeping it out of the runtime path means a tracking outage can never break serving.
nodes.tools: Here: MLflow. Same role: Weights & Biases, SageMaker or Vertex registries. Moving to a managed one is a UI change, not a concept change.
nodes.bootcampNote: You ran the MLflow server on your own laptop, with only the artifacts in S3. That kept Week 3 focused on tracking instead of hosting. A team does the same thing on a shared server or a managed platform so everyone sees one registry; nothing about your logging code would change.

nodes.what: A feature step derives the model's features from the raw usage numbers and writes the processed table. A training step fits the XGBoost model and saves it with its metrics. The whole path runs as one command, usually a thin script like train.py.
nodes.why: In the notebook this logic was scattered across cells that only worked in order, and the model lived in memory. As a pipeline, training is repeatable by anyone, and the feature code exists in exactly one place, which is what lets serving import it later instead of re-implementing it.
nodes.tools: Here: pandas, XGBoost, uv. Same role: scikit-learn pipelines; Airflow or Prefect DAGs at larger scale.

nodes.what: The trained model saved to disk in XGBoost's native format, next to a metrics file recording how good it was and on what data.
nodes.why: A model that lives only in a notebook's memory dies with the kernel. The file is what every consumer loads: the API bakes it into its container, and the batch scorer reaches it through the same function. The metrics file is the receipt.
nodes.decision: The file stays the deployment artifact even after a registry exists. What ships is a file; what remembers is the registry.
nodes.tools: Here: XGBoost JSON. Same role: pickle files, ONNX, SavedModel directories.

nodes.what: The project itself: the package, the scripts, the API, the Dockerfile, the workflow file. Everything except data, models and secrets, which are deliberately gitignored.
nodes.why: The repo is the trigger for the whole delivery path: a push to main is the only human action the deployed system needs. What is in the repo defines the system; what is gitignored defines what must be pulled from elsewhere, which is why the artifact store exists.
nodes.tools: Here: GitHub. Same role: GitLab, Bitbucket.

nodes.what: On every push: lint with ruff, pull the published model from S3, run pytest, build the Docker image. On a push to main: push the image to the registry, then SSH to the server, pull, restart, and prune the old images, so the instance never fills with layers. Secrets live in Actions secrets, never in the repo.
nodes.why: Automation of something you have already done once by hand. The first EC2 deploy is manual, so the pipeline automates a known thing instead of performing magic. The tests exist so this gate can actually fail: CI without meaningful checks is a green light bolted to nothing.
nodes.decision: Promote the image, not the code. The server never builds anything; it runs what CI built.
nodes.tools: Here: GitHub Actions. Same role: GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI.

nodes.what: The built Docker image: the API, its dependencies, and the model file CI pulled from S3, frozen into one runnable unit and pushed to GitHub Container Registry.
nodes.why: The image is the thing that gets promoted. Laptop and server run the identical artifact, which is the portability promise of containers made concrete: same image, same behavior, on any machine with Docker.
nodes.tools: Here: GHCR. Same role: Docker Hub, ECR.

nodes.what: The system's shared shelf. It holds the published model, the reference snapshot of the training data, MLflow's run artifacts, drift reports, and each night's scored list. Everything durable that is not code lives here.
nodes.why: Artifacts must survive your laptop, and services must be able to pull them from somewhere reachable. CI pulls the model from here because model files are gitignored and a fresh runner has no model otherwise. The dashboard reads everything from here. It is the quiet center of the diagram: almost every build step touches this bucket.
nodes.tools: Here: S3. Same role: GCS, Azure Blob, MinIO.

nodes.what: POST /predict takes one trial's raw usage numbers, derives features with the same feature code training used, and returns a conversion probability with a low, medium or high band. GET /health says it is alive. The model loads once at startup. It runs as a container on a small EC2 instance.
nodes.why: A trial expires in fourteen days, so a score is only useful while behavior is still accruing. Batch cadence is structurally too slow; on-demand is the honest delivery mode here. This is also where train/serve consistency is earned: serving imports the training package instead of re-implementing features.
nodes.decision: The caller sends the features in the request. Stateless, decoupled from the warehouse, a defensible v1 contract. The trial_id lookup version is the v2 discussion.
nodes.tools: Here: FastAPI, pydantic, uvicorn, Docker, EC2. Same role: Flask, BentoML, SageMaker endpoints.

nodes.what: The named humans this model exists for: the lifecycle team ranking active trials for intervention, the analytics team scoring trials mid-experiment, finance rolling up expected conversions.
nodes.why: A model is only in production when someone else can get an answer without you. Naming the consumers keeps the API honest: each one needs fresh scores mid-trial, which is why on-demand serving is a requirement in this system, not a flex.
nodes.tools: Every system has this component. If you cannot name who is in it, that is the finding.

nodes.what: Every /predict call appends one line to a log file: the features that came in, the prediction that went out, and when. Structured logging, not print statements. The drift check reads its recent lines to see what the model has actually been asked lately.
nodes.why: Labels for a day-3 prediction arrive eleven days later, so accuracy cannot be monitored live. What can be watched now is what the model is being asked and what it is answering. This log is the raw material for that, and for every "why did it say that" question afterwards.
nodes.tools: Here: JSONL on disk, synced nightly to the bucket, then truncated, because a log that lives only on one instance dies with the instance, and a log that never rotates eventually kills it. Same role: structured logs shipped to CloudWatch, a predictions table.

nodes.what: Two entries on the always-on instance: score the newest trials daily, run the drift check daily.
nodes.why: "It runs without me" is the entire point of the final build step, and cron is the smallest honest tool that delivers it. Orchestrators earn their keep when there are dependencies, retries and backfills to manage. Airflow and Prefect are industrial cron, and they come later, if ever. The honest failure mode at this scale is cron dying silently, so each job ends with a success ping, and silence itself becomes an alert.
nodes.tools: Here: cron. Same role: Airflow, Prefect, EventBridge Scheduler.

nodes.what: Runs nightly: queries the warehouse for every trial that reached day three that day, scores them all with the same predict function the API uses, and writes the ranked list to the bucket. A thin script of about twenty-five lines, because the hard part already exists.
nodes.why: The lifecycle team wants a ranked list every morning, not five hundred API calls. Recurring lists on a cadence are batch work; fresh answers mid-flight are API work. The same model serves both.
nodes.decision: Two delivery modes, one brain. Batch and on-demand import one predict function; the prediction logic is written once.
nodes.tools: Here: a Python script. Same role: Spark jobs, batch transform jobs, dbt with a model UDF.
nodes.bootcampNote: Your scorer pulls the day's cohort as a file from the course bucket instead of querying the warehouse, because the simulator delivers files. On a job, this is where the script queries the warehouse directly for yesterday's users. Same script shape, different first ten lines.

nodes.what: A daily check compares the model's recent inputs, read from the prediction log and the nightly batch, against the reference snapshot of the training data in S3, and writes two reports back: HTML for eyes, JSON for machines. Against drifted data it fires; against a healthy sample it stays quiet. It earns trust in both directions.
nodes.why: The model was fit to launch-campaign signups. When the campaign winds down and the mix shifts to lower-intent users, inputs stop looking like training data and predictions degrade silently. With labels lagging by eleven days, input drift is the early warning. It is not the verdict: once trials mature, predictions are joined back to real outcomes, and realized accuracy has the final word.
nodes.decision: Monitoring lives beside the service, not inside it. Bundling drift checks into the API would bloat the container and couple monitoring failures to serving uptime.
nodes.tools: Here: Evidently. Same role: NannyML, whylogs, SageMaker Model Monitor.

nodes.what: One page reading everything from S3: system status, the latest scored trials, the latest drift report, the model's metrics, and, once trials mature, predicted versus actual conversion.
nodes.why: Every other component answers one question; the dashboard answers "how is the whole system doing" at a glance, for people who will never SSH into anything. It is also what makes the system showable. This is the screenshot.
nodes.tools: Here: Streamlit. Same role: Grafana, Metabase, an internal admin page.

nodes.what: When the drift check flags, about ten lines of code POST a message to a Slack incoming webhook. The alert names what drifted and links the report.
nodes.why: A report nobody opens is not monitoring. The alert closes the loop: the system notices its own degradation and interrupts a human. The whole point of the finished system is exactly this message arriving while you sleep.
nodes.tools: Here: a Slack webhook. Same role: PagerDuty, Opsgenie, plain email.
nodes.bootcampNote: Your alerts land in your own channel in the course Slack, because you can't install webhook apps in a workspace you don't admin. On a job the webhook points at your team's workspace and the same ten lines of code page whoever is on call.

train.title: Train the model
train.desc: The path a model takes from a warehouse table to a published artifact.

hops.t: A small fetch script pulls the trial snapshot once and saves it to the project's data directory, stamped with its date.
The feature step derives the model's features from the raw usage numbers and writes the processed table.
The training step fits XGBoost and saves the model file plus its metrics. The model now exists outside anyone's memory.
The run's parameters, metrics and artifact are logged, so this exact model stays citable later.
The chosen model is published to the bucket. Everything downstream pulls it from here, never from a laptop.
The training extract is published alongside it as the reference snapshot: the system will need to remember what normal looked like.

ship.title: Push to production
ship.desc: A change on main redeploys the system with no hands on a server.

hops.t: A change lands on main. Actions wakes up and lints the code.
The runner has no model, because model files are gitignored. CI pulls the published model from S3 first, then the tests can run.
ruff and pytest pass. The image is built, model baked in, and pushed to the registry.
CD connects to the server, pulls the new image and restarts the container. The server never builds anything; it runs what CI built.

request.title: Score one trial, live
request.desc: What happens in the milliseconds after someone needs an answer.

hops.t: A lifecycle manager needs today's answer for a trial on its third day and sends its usage numbers to POST /predict.
The service derives features with the same code training used and returns a probability plus a low, medium or high band.
The call is appended to the prediction log: features in, prediction out, timestamp. Monitoring reads this later.

batch.title: The nightly batch
batch.desc: The lifecycle team's ranked list appears every morning without anyone asking.

hops.t: All day, users try the product and their events land in the warehouse. By nightfall, another batch of trials has reached day three.
cron fires the score script on schedule.
The batch scorer queries the warehouse for every trial that reached day three today and scores them with the same predict function the API imports. One brain, two delivery modes.
The scored, ranked list is written to the bucket: the lifecycle team's morning list.
The dashboard picks up the new scores. The system reported its own work.

drift.title: Drift fires an alert
drift.desc: The launch campaign winds down, the signup mix shifts, and the system notices before any label could.

hops.t: cron runs the daily drift check.
The reference snapshot comes in from the bucket: the training data, the world exactly as the model learned it.
Recent inputs come from the prediction log. The acquisition mix has shifted to lower-intent signups; inputs no longer look like training data.
The report writes to the bucket: HTML for eyes, JSON for machines. This one flags.
The webhook fires. The alert lands in Slack while you sleep. The system caught its own degradation.

skew.title: The model goes quietly wrong
skew.desc: Nothing crashes and nothing alerts. The service simply starts computing a feature one way and handing it to a model that learned it another.

hops.t: You change how one feature is computed, from every session in the trial's first three days to the number of distinct days it was active, and retrain. The metrics come back better. This is the model you want serving.
You publish it to the bucket, over the file that was already there. The code that computes the feature the new way is still on your branch.
hops.note: Nothing is wrong yet. This is only the step that makes it possible: the model reaches production through the bucket, the code reaches it through git, and nothing makes the two arrive together.

hops.t: Two days later an unrelated fix lands on main. CI pulls the published model, which is now yours, and the tests run against it. Everything passes, because the code agrees with itself and no test asks whether this model was trained by this code.
The image is built and pushed: the old feature code and the new model, frozen into one container that looks exactly like every release before it.
The server pulls it and restarts. A green deploy. Every check this system has says it is healthy, and by every check this system has, it is.

A request arrives. The service counts sessions, the way its code still does, and hands that number to a model that learned distinct active days. Same field name, same type, a perfectly plausible range. The model splits on it happily and answers 0.83, high band. There is nothing here to raise an error about.
The call is logged like any other: features in, prediction out, timestamp. Read the log and this day looks like every day before it.

The daily drift check compares what is arriving against the reference snapshot. But what arrives, the raw usage numbers the caller sends, never changed. The shift happened after that, inside the container. Drift is watching the door, and the mistake is in the kitchen.

skew.ending:
What finally catches it

Eleven days later the first trials from that release mature into real outcomes, and predicted versus actual on the dashboard is worse than the metrics that convinced you to ship. By then two weeks of ranked lists have gone to the lifecycle team, and nobody suspects the deploy, because the deploy was green.

What would have caught it sooner

Stamp the model with the git commit that trained it, and have the service refuse to start when that is not the commit it is running. The model and the code lose the ability to arrive separately, which is the actual bug. Two cheaper habits help too: publish the model from CI rather than from a laptop, and log the derived features next to the raw inputs, so the drift check watches the numbers the model is really fed.

Serving imports the training package here, which is the right design and is exactly why this is easy to miss. Train/serve consistency is a property of the model and the code together, not of either one alone.

buildSteps.title: A notebook becomes a project
buildSteps.text: The prototype notebook is migrated into a structured, script-runnable project. Data is pulled once from the warehouse and frozen; training runs from the command line; the model and its metrics land on disk as files.
buildSteps.you: This week your notebook became a real project. You pulled the data once and froze it, moved training into scripts that run from the command line, and your model and its metrics now land on disk as files, with everything in version control.
buildSteps.decision: Train from a materialized extract, never from the live table. Reproducibility beats freshness at training time.

buildSteps.title: The model becomes a service
buildSteps.text: Prediction logic is written once in the package, wrapped in a FastAPI service, and shipped as a Docker container. Anyone can POST a trial's numbers and get a probability back.
buildSteps.you: This week your model became a service. You wrote the prediction logic once in your package, wrapped it in a FastAPI service, and shipped it in a Docker container. Anyone can now POST a trial's numbers to your API and get a probability back.
buildSteps.decision: The caller sends features in the request. Stateless, decoupled from the warehouse, an honest v1 contract.

buildSteps.title: Experiments become citable
buildSteps.text: Every training run is tracked, the best model is registered as a named version, and artifacts move to S3, where they survive laptops and become reachable by machines.
buildSteps.you: This week your experiments became citable. Every training run you make is tracked, your best model is registered as a named version, and your artifacts moved to S3, where they survive laptops and are reachable by machines.
buildSteps.decision: The model file stays the deployment artifact. The registry is the system of record, not a runtime dependency.

buildSteps.title: Deploys become a push
buildSteps.text: The container moves to a real server, and GitHub Actions takes over the path from push to production: lint, pull the model, test, build, ship, restart.
buildSteps.you: This week your deploys became a push. Your container moved to a real server, and GitHub Actions now owns the path from your push to production: lint, pull the model, test, build, ship, restart.
buildSteps.decision: Promote the image, not the code. The server never builds anything; it runs what CI built.

buildSteps.title: Silence becomes signal
buildSteps.text: The service starts logging every prediction, and a drift check compares incoming data against the training extract. With labels eleven days away, inputs are the only early warning available.
buildSteps.you: This week silence became signal. Your service now logs every prediction, and your drift check compares incoming data against the training extract. With labels eleven days away, inputs are your only early warning.
buildSteps.decision: When labels lag, monitor inputs and predictions. Drift checks live beside the service, never inside it.

buildSteps.title: The system runs without you
buildSteps.text: cron schedules scoring and drift checks on the always-on instance, alerts reach Slack on their own, and one dashboard shows the whole system's state. The builder is no longer in the loop.
buildSteps.you: This week the system started running without you. cron runs your scoring and drift checks on the always-on instance, alerts reach Slack on their own, and your dashboard shows the whole system's state. You are no longer in the loop, and that was the point.
buildSteps.decision: Two delivery modes, one brain. Batch and on-demand both import the same predict function.

tour.title: A model in production is a promise
body: In a notebook, a model gives you one answer, once. In production, it has to keep answering: anyone can ask for a fresh prediction on any day, and you won't be there to run it.

The model we'll follow predicts which free trials will convert to paid. Over the next few steps, we'll walk through the four stages of the system around it: making the model, shipping it, running it and watching it.
tour.why: Each stage replaces a job you would otherwise have to do by hand, again and again.

tour.title: Freeze the data, then script the training
body: We start by pulling the trial data from the warehouse once and saving it as a dated file. That file is a fixed snapshot we can always come back to, even after the warehouse table changes.
Training then runs from that file as a script, not as notebook cells. At the end, you have a model file on disk with its metrics saved next to it.
tour.why: If you run the same script on the same file next month, you get the same model. Training from a live table could never promise that.

moments.text: First, a fetch script pulls the trial data from the warehouse once and saves it as a dated file.
From that frozen file, a feature step builds the model's inputs, and training fits XGBoost and saves the model with its metrics.

tour.title: Every experiment becomes citable
body: Next, we record each training run in MLflow, with its settings, its metrics and the model it produced. When we're happy with a run, we register that model as a named version.
Then we copy the model and the data snapshot to an S3 bucket. That way they no longer depend on your laptop, and the other machines in the system can reach them.
tour.why: When someone asks which model is live and why, you can answer with a link instead of relying on your memory.

moments.text: The run is logged to MLflow: its settings, its metrics and the model, so this exact model can be cited later.
The chosen model is published to S3, along with the training data as a reference snapshot. Everything downstream pulls from there.

tour.title: A push to main becomes a running server
body: Now we get the model onto a server. When a change lands on main, GitHub Actions takes over: it lints the code, pulls the model from S3, runs the tests and builds a Docker image with the model inside.
The server then pulls the new image and restarts. Nobody logs into the server to build anything by hand.
tour.why: Deploying stops being a special event. It simply happens every time you push to main.

moments.text: A change lands on main. GitHub Actions lints it, then pulls the published model from S3, because model files are not in git.
The tests pass, and CI builds a Docker image with the model inside and pushes it to the registry.
The server pulls the new image and restarts. It never builds anything itself; it runs what CI built.

tour.title: Score one trial, live
body: With the server running, let's follow one request. A lifecycle manager sends a trial's usage numbers to the prediction service and gets back a probability, plus a band of low, medium or high.
Every call is also logged, with the features that went in, the prediction that came out and the time it happened.
tour.why: We'll come back to that log later, because it's what lets the system check itself.

moments.text: A lifecycle manager sends a trial's usage numbers to POST /predict and gets back a probability and a band.
The call is logged: features in, prediction out, timestamp. Monitoring will read this later.

tour.title: Score every trial, every night
body: Not everyone needs answers one trial at a time. Every night, cron starts a batch job that scores every trial that reached day three and writes a ranked list for the team to read in the morning.
The batch job uses the same predict function as the live service, so both give the same answer for the same trial.
tour.why: If the prediction logic lived in two places, the two copies would slowly drift apart. Keeping a single copy avoids that.

moments.text: All day, user events land in the warehouse. At night, cron starts the batch scoring job.
The scorer scores every trial that reached day three, using the same predict function as the live API.
The ranked list is written to S3 for the team's morning, and the dashboard picks up the new scores.

tour.title: The system notices when the world shifts
body: Now for watching. The real outcome of a trial only arrives 11 days later, which is too late to warn anyone. So instead, a daily check compares today's inputs with the data the model was trained on.
When the mix of signups shifts, the check writes a report and posts an alert to Slack without anyone having to ask.
tour.why: That way, you find out about the problem before your users do.

moments.text: Every day, cron runs the drift check, which loads the reference snapshot: the data the model learned from.
It compares that with recent inputs from the prediction log. The signup mix has shifted, so inputs no longer look like training data.
It writes a report to S3 and posts an alert to Slack, on its own.

tour.title: Wrong, without a single error
body: This last flow shows a failure the system can't catch. Someone changes how a feature is computed and retrains the model, but the old feature code ships with the new model. Every test still passes, the deploy is green, and the drift check sees nothing unusual.
From then on, the model quietly scores trials using a number it never learned from.
tour.why: The fix is to stamp each model with the commit that trained it, and to refuse to serve a model whose commit doesn't match the running code.

moments.text: You change how one feature is computed, retrain, and publish the better model to S3. The new feature code is still on your branch.
Days later an unrelated fix triggers CI. It pulls your new model, every test passes, and the old code and new model ship together.
A request arrives. The service computes the feature the old way, and the model happily answers 0.83. No error.
The call is logged like any other, and the drift check sees normal inputs, because the shift happens inside the container. No alert fires.

tour.title: Everything you just saw, in one picture

recap.make: We froze the data in a dated file, scripted the training, tracked every run in MLflow and published the model to S3.
recap.ship: A push to main lints, tests and builds an image with the model inside, and the server pulls it and restarts.
recap.run: The same predict function answers live requests and scores every trial overnight.
recap.watch: Every call is logged, and a daily check compares new inputs with the training data and alerts Slack when they drift.

body: That's the full loop: we make the model, ship it, run it and watch it. Each stage takes a person out of a job they would otherwise repeat by hand.
This is the whole system on one map, and you've now seen why every component on it is there.

ci.title: Inside the CI/CD pipeline
ci.sub: What actually happens between git push and a live server.
ci.cap: The first five steps run on every push, on every branch. The last two run only when main changes. Note the model pull: the runner starts empty because model files are gitignored, so the published artifact comes from S3 before the tests or the image build can succeed.

api.title: Inside the prediction service
api.sub: One container, one loaded model, one prediction function shared with the whole system.
api.cap: The container is the unit that ships. Inside it, FastAPI handles the HTTP layer and pydantic validates the request shape, but the actual prediction comes from the package's own predict function, the same one the nightly batch scorer imports. Train/serve consistency is not an aspiration here; it is an import statement.

s3.title: Inside the bucket
s3.sub: Four prefixes, and who reads and writes each one.
s3.cap: One bucket, four jobs, and one typical way to name the prefixes. Nothing here is code, and everything here outlives any single machine. When someone asks where the system keeps its state, this is the answer.

mlflow.title: Inside experiment tracking
mlflow.sub: Three runs, one registered winner, artifacts stored where machines can reach them.
mlflow.cap: The registry answers 'which model is in production and how was it trained'. But note what production actually loads: the plain model.json published to S3. The registry remembers; the file ships. That separation keeps the serving path free of a runtime dependency on MLflow.

train.title: Inside the training pipeline
train.sub: Files in, files out, one command end to end.
train.cap: One typical way this lays out on disk; the names matter less than the shape. Each step reads files and writes files, which is what makes the pipeline restartable and debuggable. The processed table is persisted deliberately: production needs to inspect what the model actually trained on, and the notebook never kept that.

drift.title: Inside the drift check
drift.sub: Reference versus reality, statistics in between, and an alert only when it matters.
drift.cap: The reference is the original training extract: the world as the model learned it. Every day, the newest data is compared against it, feature by feature. The HTML report is for human eyes; the JSON twin is for the alerting logic, which posts to Slack only when the tests flag. Run against a healthy sample, it stays quiet, which is what makes it trustworthy.
